sources.title: Triangulating the origin of the Transeurasian languages
sources.note: A prominent multidisciplinary argument for a Transeurasian family and farming-linked dispersal, useful as one side of an active controversy.

sources.title: Triangulation fails when neither linguistic, genetic, nor archaeological data support the Transeurasian narrative
sources.note: Detailed scholarly critique arguing that linguistic, archaeological and genetic evidence does not establish the proposed family or dispersal narrative.

sources.title: The End of the Altaic Controversy, bibliographic record
sources.note: Glottolog record for Alexander Vovin’s comparative-historical critique of the Altaic etymological reconstruction.

sources.title: Telling general linguists about Altaic
sources.note: A published defense showing that Altaic has serious scholarly advocates as well as critics and should be presented as debated.

sources.title: Permutation test applied to lexical reconstructions partially supports the Altaic linguistic macrofamily
sources.note: Quantitative lexical study reporting partial statistical support while acknowledging contact and unresolved interpretation.

sources.title: A Sketch of the Earliest Mongolic Language
sources.note: Study dating securely interpreted early Mongolic Bugut and Khuis Tolgoi texts to the sixth and early seventh centuries CE, far later than this card.

sources.title: Literature of the Turkic Peoples
sources.note: UNESCO history placing surviving Old Turkic inscriptional literature centuries after the atlas interval.

sources.title: Bronze Age population dynamics and the rise of dairy pastoralism on the eastern Eurasian steppe
sources.note: Ancient genomes and milk proteins show local northern Mongolian ancestry alongside adopted sheep, goat and cattle dairying by about 1300 BCE.

sources.title: Dairy pastoralism sustained Eastern Eurasian Steppe populations for 5000 years
sources.note: Dental calculus proteomics traces ruminant dairy and horse milk consumption while emphasizing regional and chronological differences.

sources.title: Early Pastoral Economies and Herding Transitions in Eastern Eurasia
sources.note: Habitation fauna, structures, horses and transport evidence distinguish changing pastoral economies rather than one timeless nomadic package.

sources.title: A Dynamic 6,000-Year Genetic History of Eurasia’s Eastern Steppe
sources.note: More than 200 ancient genomes reveal repeated mixture and several genetically distinct Bronze Age groups that shared dairy pastoralism.

sources.title: Radiocarbon dating and cultural dynamics across Mongolia’s early pastoral transition
sources.note: Bayesian modeling clarifies overlapping monument traditions and the late second-millennium expansion of horse-centered practices.

sources.title: Slab Grave expansion disrupted long co-existence of distinct Bronze Age herders in central Mongolia
sources.note: New genome-wide evidence separates several herding populations and documents later Slab Grave expansion rather than a single continuous ethnic block.

sources.title: 3000 yr-old patterns of mobile pastoralism revealed by multiple isotopes and radiocarbon dating of ancient horses
sources.note: Horse tooth isotopes reconstruct repeated movements and suggest that seven deposited horses included a mobile herd managed by a small community.

sources.title: The spread of herds and horses into the Altai
sources.note: Proteomics links long-term ruminant dairying, later horse milk and growing monumentality in western Mongolia.

sources.title: Deer Stone Monuments and Related Bronze Age Sites
sources.note: UNESCO synthesis of 1200 to 600 BCE deer stones, khirigsuurs, horse remains, ceremonial landscapes and extraordinary carved art.

sources.title: Joint Mongolian-Smithsonian Deer Stone Project
sources.note: Institutional field-project overview of carved standing stones, Khövsgöl research and association with stone burial mounds.

sources.title: The Mongolian Deer Stone-Khirigsuur Complex
sources.note: Excavation synthesis of monument plans, shallow human graves, east-facing horse deposits, hearths, feasting remains and preservation limits.

sources.title: Horse sacrifice and butchery in Bronze Age Mongolia
sources.note: Smithsonian record for cut-mark and skeletal analysis demonstrating slaughter, dismemberment and meat removal in ritual horse deposits.

sources.title: Horse demography and use in Bronze Age Mongolia
sources.note: Age and sex profiles of DSK horses support managed breeding herds and transport use while documenting sample limitations.

sources.title: Origins of equine dentistry
sources.note: Directly dated horse teeth show attempted dental care around 1150 BCE and later wolf-tooth extraction alongside metal bits.

sources.title: A palaeopathological analysis of skeletal remains from Bronze Age Mongolia
sources.note: Study of 25 northern Mongolian people reports limited visible disease but trauma and joint changes consistent with violence and riding.

sources.title: Bronze Age Mongolia
sources.note: Scholarly synthesis of regional chronologies, sparse settlement evidence, seasonal camps, mixed herds, monuments and uncertain social hierarchy.

sources.title: Socially Integrative Facilities and the Emergence of Societal Complexity on the Mongolian Steppe
sources.note: Analysis of how large ritual facilities could coordinate mobile communities without presuming a centralized territorial state.

sources.title: Economic Diversification Supported the Growth of Mongolia’s Nomadic Empires
sources.note: Stable-isotope evidence shows increasing millet consumption from about 800 BCE and warns against imagining all steppe diets as identical.

sources.title: Intensification in pastoralist cereal use coincides with the expansion of trans-regional networks
sources.note: Broad isotope and seed study finds cereal uptake varied strongly, with intensive millet use delayed in Mongolia until late in the first millennium BCE.

sources.title: Ancient bronze technology and nomadic communities of the Middle Gobi Desert
sources.note: Metallographic study identifies casting debris, slag, local or regional production and long-distance objects across pre-Xiongnu and Xiongnu contexts.

sources.title: Nomadic Art of the Eastern Eurasian Steppes
sources.note: Museum overview of portable bronze, gold, silver and jade harness fittings, belt ornaments, garment plaques, weapons and vessels.

sources.title: High altitude hunting, climate change, and pastoral resilience in eastern Eurasia
sources.note: Ice-patch archaeology recovers organic hunting evidence and shows wild resources remained important within herding economies.

sources.title: Investigating reindeer pastoralism and exploitation of high mountain zones in northern Mongolia
sources.note: Glacial archaeology demonstrates preservation bias and cautions against projecting historically known reindeer herding unchanged into the Bronze Age.

sources.title: Petroglyphic Complexes of the Mongolian Altai
sources.note: UNESCO account of rock art showing long environmental change, herding, hunting and later horse-dependent mobility.

sources.title: Petroglyphic Complexes in the Mongolian Gobi
sources.note: Institutional description of riders, herds, hunts, carts and rare cultivation scenes in a multi-period rock-art landscape.

sources.title: ICOMOS evaluation of Deer Stone Monuments
sources.note: Expert assessment of dating, integrity, looting, landscape relationships and limits of interpretation for the monument complexes.

sources.title: Tracking Five Millennia of Horse Management with Extensive Ancient Genome Time Series
sources.note: Ancient horse genomes document changing managed lineages and directly sampled animals from Uushgiin Uvur and later Mongolian sites.

sources.title: The earliest Bronze Age culture of the eastern Eurasian steppe
sources.note: Peer-reviewed regional synthesis emphasizing long-lived hunter-gatherer traditions, cultural diversity and gradual development of pastoral networks.

sources.title: Tracing the flows of copper and copper alloys in Early Iron Age eastern Eurasian steppe societies
sources.note: University research on ore sources, alloy recipes, primary metal movement, recycling and secondary circulation across steppe networks.

sources.title: Burning Resources: Traditional Fuel Uses on the Mongolian Steppe
sources.note: Ethnoarchaeological study of wood, bone and dung fuel that offers cautious analogies for interpreting sparse domestic combustion evidence.

sources.title: Report of the Khanuy Valley Archaeology Project
sources.note: Multidisciplinary field report targeting habitation areas, faunal remains, plants, sediments and camp structure near monuments.

proposedOverrides.summary: A disputed atlas umbrella over many Bronze and Early Iron Age communities. Archaeology shows varied regional herding, hunting, dairying, riding, craft and monument traditions, not one Proto-Altaic people or state.
